newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada say Cuba dispute will not disrupt ties.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada say Cuba dispute will not disrupt ties.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien agreed on Tuesday not to let a dispute over Cuba policy colour otherwise strong ties between the United States and Canada.

Chretien, on a reciprocal visit to Washington after Clinton visited Ottawa two years ago, was given rare treatment for a foreign visitor -- Clinton had him over for a glass of cognac and a private chat Monday night ahead of Tuesday's colourful White House arrival ceremony and official business.

The two sides were expected to mark the visit with agreements on border-related issues, trade and environmental protection. Canada is the United States' biggest trading partner, with exchanges valued at $1 billion a day.
In an otherwise sunny relationship, the United States and Canada are at odds over Cuba. Canada strongly protests the U.S. anti-Castro Helms-Burton Act.

Chretien was expected to again press Clinton to get rid of the law, which punishes some companies in third countries that do business in Cuba, or at least to continue to suspend one of its key provisions. Canada has strong trade and investment ties with Cuba.

"We just have a different approach here and we'll try to find a way to manage our differences," Clinton told reporters during an Oval Office picture-taking session as he and Chretien sat down for their talks.
Chretien, commenting on the overall state of U.S.-Canadian relations, said: "When you look at it, we manage to solve most of the problems in a very nice way."
Clinton said he and Chretien would also discuss plans for NATO expansion, Haiti and Bosnia as well as bilateral issues.
One topic neither side seemed eager to raise was the touchy issue of the status of the French-speaking province of Quebec within Canada.

Quebec was not mentioned by the leaders before the talks started, and White House spokesman Mike McCurry was careful to restate only the offical U.S. government mantra: "We enjoy good relations with a strong and united Canada."

Quebec separatists nearly won a 1995 provincial referendum on autonomy from Canada that could have torn the country apart, and Chretien, a French-speaking Quebecker himself, was severely criticised for his handling of the issue.

One agreement expected between the two countries, a Canadian official said, would be to develop a joint plan of action to cut down on trans-border smog -- especially low-level ozone and small particles.

He said the idea would be for cuts of about 50 percent or more, although no targets would be set in next week's agreement. Canada says more than half the smog in the central Ontario-Quebec border area comes from the United States.
A second pact would provide for the "virtual elimination" from the Great Lakes of toxic substances like PCBs and dioxins.
A third agreement will pledge work on protecting endangered species like grizzly bears that cross the border.

Another deal, symbolic of the goal to improve trans-border flows, will provide for Asian passengers transiting through Vancouver airport to the United States to go directly through U.S. customs in Vancouver and avoid Canadian customs.

Some Canadian commentators suggested Chretien timed the visit to look prime ministerial ahead of general elections he could call for June or October. Chretien's camp dismisses that argument. But his Liberal party is well ahead in public opinion polls more than a year before his mandate expires.
Even on the traditionally thorny issue of trade disputes between the two neighbours ranging from wheat to lumber and magazine publishing, Chretien struck a conciliatory tone.

"We have managed to resolve most of the difficulties. When we started we had 5 percent of our trade in dispute, and now it's down to 1 percent... We have mananged to talk to each other and have very good relations," he said.
